title: Shavuot: milk and greenery
hookLine: dairy meals, and greenery in homes and synagogues

cards: Blintzes. Cheesecake. A noodle kugel heavy with cottage cheese.
In some Sephardi kitchens, little cheese pastries, or rice cooked in milk. A festival that remembers a desert mountain, thunder and the giving of the Torah, and the menu looks like a dairy aisle.

Then look up: branches over the doorways, flowers on the table, and in some synagogues leafy boughs beside the ark, or roses wound around the reading table. Nobody in the Torah's account of Sinai eats a blintz.
So where did all this come from?

teach.b: Shavuot means weeks: seven weeks counted from Passover, then this festival. The Torah gives it a harvest face, the feast of the first fruits of the wheat; the rabbis gave it a second, the day the Torah was given.
The Torah says nothing about cheese, and nobody can point to the day the custom started. Instead there's a pile of explanations, offered side by side.

teach.h: MILK: SWEET AS TORAH, OR FORTY DAYS.
teach.b: One reaches for the Song of Songs, which speaks of honey and milk under the tongue; the rabbis read that as the Torah, sweet and nourishing.
A second is practical: once the laws of kosher food were given at Sinai, the story goes, nobody had properly prepared meat or pots ready, so they ate dairy.
A third is a number game: Hebrew letters are numbers, and chalav, milk, adds up to forty, the days Moses spent on the mountain.

A fourth is a pun, told with a smile: a psalm calls a mountain gavnunim, many-peaked, which sounds like gevinah, cheese. Now the green. A common explanation says bare Sinai burst into bloom when the Torah was given.
Some point to Exodus: the flocks were told not to graze in front of the mountain, so there must have been grass.
Others connect it to a teaching in the Mishnah that on Shavuot the world is judged for the fruit of the trees.
Not every community does it: some, following the Vilna Gaon, leave trees out of the synagogue; others fill it with flowers.
A teaching that came down a mountain in fire is remembered with food that nourishes and leaves that grow.

how: On Shavuot it is a widespread custom to eat dairy meals, such as blintzes and cheesecake, and decorate homes and synagogues with greenery and flowers; some communities, following the Vilna Gaon, do not bring trees into the synagogue.

games.q: it's the day after Sinai. the laws of kosher food have just been given, and nothing in the camp has been prepared for them. what's for dinner?
o: dairy, with no meat or pots to prepare.
games.why: one of the explanations people give: with no properly prepared meat or pots ready, they ate dairy. it's an explanation, not a verse.

practice: Set something green in front of you, a sprig, a leaf, a stem of mint, a houseplant, and look at the way the stem carries water out to the edges.
Think of one thing you were given, a lesson, a habit, a sentence someone said, that kept growing in you long after it was handed over.

wordCard.voice: Shavuot. Weeks: the festival seven weeks after Passover, of first fruits and the Torah given, kept with dairy meals and greenery. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: milk. chet, lamed, bet: eight, thirty, two, adding up to forty.

carryVoice: Your line: green and milk. What we're given is meant to feed us, and to grow. That's day six hundred ninety-two.
